extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of philosophy and epistemology (general educated public interested in theories of ideas and innateness)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and argumentative tests for whether a maxim, moral rule, or proposition should be regarded as innate (originally imprinted on the mind) versus acquired by experience, education, or reflection. The text lists and critiques the marks commonly offered for innateness (universal assent, first-hearing assent, presence in children, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assenting as soon as proposed and understood
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that ready assent given to a proposition upon first hearing and understanding the terms is a mark that the proposition is innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defenders of innate ideas use 'assent at first hearing' as a test. The text objects that many propositions (e.g., arithmetic truths like 'one and two are equal to three', sensory oppositions like 'sweetness is not bitterness', metaphysical truths such as 'it is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be') also receive immediate assent when understood, so this mark would promiscuously classify many acquired or learned propositions as innate. Thus first-hearing assent shows self-evidence but not necessarily innateness; examples and anti-patterns include arithmetic, simple contradictions, and many natural-philosophical propositions that meet the same test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal assent
rubrics_metrics.description: If a truth is innate, it must have universal assent — every rational person (and those capable of understanding) should assent to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists that innate truths must be universally assented to; since many alleged innate maxims are not assented to by children, certain classes of people, or large portions of mankind, they fail this test. Hume uses the lack of assent among children, idiots, savages, and many adults unfamiliar with abstract ideas as evidence against innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known before any teaching or proposal (no precedent teaching)
rubrics_metrics.description: An innate principle should not require being proposed or taught in order to gain assent; it should be known prior to explicit instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues this is a mistaken supposition: many propositions are only assented to after their terms and the relevant ideas are learned. The fact that some truths are better known after being proposed suggests they are not naturally inscribed but are learned; examples include children who only assent to certain propositions once they have the relevant ideas and names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present and clearest in children, idiots, and uncorrupted minds
rubrics_metrics.description: If characters/principles were native impressions, they should be most visible in those least influenced by education, habit, or custom (children, idiots, savages, and the grossly illiterate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text holds that innate impressions should 'shine out' strongest in uncorrupted minds, yet such groups typically lack the general maxims claimed to be innate. Their limited notions come from immediate sensory experience rather than abstract maxims, which suggests those maxims are not innate but products of schooling and learned discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earliest known in the mind (first of any thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate truths should be the first thoughts and earliest known principles in the mind; they ought to precede acquired notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues that many alleged innate maxims are not the first cognitions of children (who know particular things earlier), so they cannot be innate. The child’s early knowledge of concrete relations (nurse vs. cat, apple vs. wormseed) comes prior to abstract maxims, contradicting the requirement that innate truths be foremost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit knowledge prior to explicit awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenders sometimes claim a distinction between implicit (in the understanding) and explicit knowledge (conscious awareness), claiming principles are implicitly present before being explicitly known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes this move as vacuous: to claim implicit knowledge merely amounts to saying the mind is capable of understanding those propositions, not that the ideas themselves are literally imprinted. If implicit knowledge were taken to imply innate characters, then complex mathematical knowledge would have to be counted innate — an implausible consequence. The argument reduces to capacity rather than actual innate impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-evidence (needs no proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate principles must be self-evident: they carry their own light and need no external proof to be accepted once understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text differentiates speculative maxims (which are self-evident) from moral rules (which typically require reasoning). Moral rules such as 'do as you would be done unto' can be and are reasonably asked for reasons; their needing proof indicates they are not self-evident innate truths. Hume gives the exemplar that one can coherently ask why one must keep compacts, showing moral maxims lack the self-evidence required of innate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate practical principles must constantly influence action
rubrics_metrics.description: If practical (moral) principles are innate, they should operate continuously and influence conduct uniformly in all persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contends that only appetitive inclinations (desire of happiness, aversion to misery) meet this condition; purported innate moral rules do not consistently shape actions. Hume points to widespread violations of moral rules (robberies, murders, exposure of children, culturally sanctioned cruelties) and the fact that outlaws nonetheless keep certain rules among themselves for convenience, showing that outward conformity often owes to interest or social utility rather than innate moral conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity across societies (not publicly rejected by whole nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a principle were innate it could not be publicly rejected or renounced by an entire society; it should be recognized across cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues that whole nations have and do reject or practice contrary moral rules (e.g., exposure or killing of children, cannibalism, differing notions about duels). Such cultural diversity and public rejection of purported moral principles indicate they are not innate but contingent, social, or learned.
